speakeroldname: Mr. Eldon M. Woolliams (Bow River) moved
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TRIAL AND CONFINEMENT OF MINORS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-121, to amend the Criminal Code.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TRIAL AND CONFINEMENT OF MINORS
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TRIAL AND CONFINEMENT OF MINORS
speechtext:
This bill is an amendment to the Criminal Code in reference to sections
12	and 13.
The amendment will raise the age from 7 to 10 years in reference to the legal right to charge and convict a minor, with a proviso that no person shall be convicted of any offence under the code between the ages of 10 and 16 years of age, unless he is competent to know the nature and consequence of his conduct and, above all, to appreciate that his conduct was wrong.
In order to put an end to incarcerating children in penitentiaries as young as 12 and
13	years of age, clause 13(A) was added, which will set out that no person under the age of 16 years, if convicted of an offence, can be placed in a penitentiary and, if an

offence was such that under the circumstances a person who was under 16 years of age would be sentenced to a penitentiary, then such person would be confined to an industrial school for the purpose of rehabilitation.
In brief, the amendment will prevent children between the ages of 7 and 10 years from being convicted of any offence, and children of 16 years and under from being placed in penitentiaries.
As late as December 31, 1963 there were 45 children in penitentiaries, 16 years of age and under, and 386 under the age of 18 years.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF JAMAICA
speechtext:
1. The communique issued at the close of the discussions between the Prime Minister and the Acting Prime Minister of Jamaica, November 29, 1965, was as follows:
The Prime Minister of Canada, Right Hon. Lester Pearson, and the Acting Prime Minister of Jamaica, Hon. Donald Sangster, yesterday discussed a wide range of subjects of interest to their two countries. They also discussed the world political situation, paying special attention to the critical situation in Rhodesia.
Assisting Mr. Sangster in the discussion were other members of the Jamaica cabinet as well as government officials. Mr. Pearson was assisted by his advisers and the Canadian High Commissioner in Jamaica, Mr. R. Harry Jay.
On Rhodesia Mr. Pearson and Mr. Sangster shared a deep concern over the situation resulting from the unilateral declaration of independence by the Smith regime. Mr. Pearson described the various trade and financial measures being taken by Canada, following consultation within the Commonwealth and the deliberations of the U.N., including the recent ban on all importation into Canada of sugar of Rhodesian origin. Mr. Sangster expressed his concern that economic measures might not prove fully effective. Mr. Pearson and Mr. Sangster agreed on the importance of keeping in close touch over developments in this deplorable and dangerous situation.
The Prime Ministers also discussed various other international questions including issues currently confronting the United Nations and developments in the O.A.S.
The Prime Minister of Canada expressed the support of his government for Jamaica's peacekeeping initiative in the United Nations.
On the question of aid, the Acting Prime Minister reaffirmed the gratitude of the Jamaican government to Canada for the generous terms of Canadian aid. Different aspects of the loans and technical assistance programs were discussed and a number of proposals examined.
Much of today's discussion related to trade and economic topics. The progress being made in the current tariff negotiations in Geneva was reviewed and arrangements were made to consult closely on aspects of these negotiations of special interest to the two countries. The importance to Jamaica of
February 9, 1966

sugar exports to Canada was stressed and the interest of the two governments in the achievement of an effective international sugar agreement was recognized.
Other specific trade problems were examined, such as the current negotiations regarding codfish purchases and the sale of rum to Canada.
Proposals which had been made earlier for a Canada-West Indies conference were also discussed. Mr. Pearson and Mr. Sangster agreed that further exploratory and preparatory discussions should take place in the very near future between representatives of all governments concerned.
The Prime Ministers examined the question of migration of Jamaican domestic and other labour to Canada as well as the general question of Jamaican immigration to Canada.
They reaffirmed their desire to find solutions to the problems discussed in such a way that the very close relationship between their countries would be maintained and strengthened.
The discussions took place in a most cordial atmosphere with both Prime Ministers appreciating each other's point of view.

The Prime Minister of Canada, Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, arrived in Trinidad on December 14 on a two day official visit.
Today, December 15, the Prime Minister of Canada conferred with the Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago on a number of subjects of mutual interest to both countries. The Prime Minister of Canada was accompanied by Mr. A. E. Ritchie, deputy under-secretary of state for external affairs, and Mr. Eric Gilmour, High Commissioner for Canada. With the Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago were Senator the Hon. W. J. Alexander, Minister without Portfolio and special adviser to the Prime Minister; Hon. G. Montano, Minister of Home Affairs; Hon. J. O'Halloran, Minister of Petroleum and Mines and Minister of Industry and Commerce; Senator the Hon. Donald Pierre, Minister of Education and Culture. The Prime Ministers discussed the international situation and paid special attention to the serious situation which has arisen as a consequence of the illegal seizure of power by the regime in Southern Rhodesia.
The Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago paid tribute to the government of Canada for their liberal attitude in their policy of grants and loans offered to Trinidad and Tobago and expressed his appreciation of the work now being done in Trinidad and Tobago by technical advisers and more particularly the work of teachers in the secondary schools and other educational institutions.
The Prime Minister of Canada expressed the willingness of his government to extend the assistance in the field of education during the coming year.
The discussions also included a reference to some aspects of the terms of economic aid. The Prime Minister also discussed the tariff negotiations now going on in Geneva and the trade of developing countries. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DELIVERIES OF GRAIN TO VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Prior to entering into the sales contract for Canadian wheat and flour with the U.S.S.R. last August, a meeting was held between the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the presidents of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway, and the Canadian Wheat Board to assess rail transportation requirements for the massive grain movement envisaged. At that time the Canadian Wheat Board estimated total wheat and flour exports for the crop year at 600 million bushels, just slightly in excess of the record movement of 596 million bushels achieved in 1963-64. A movement of this magnitude would make possible the achievement of the proposed contract with the U.S.S.R. as well as all commitments under long term agreements and purchases by traditional customers.
With some qualifications about the rapid turn around of their equipment, high moisture content of the grain which could slow down the movement, and the necessity of their operations not being unduly restricted by wheat board quota policies, both railways indicated that the commitments envisaged by the wheat board could be met.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. May I thank the minister, too, because I feel that what I have to say this afternoon is most important, not only to the area which I represent but to the country as a whole. I wish this afternoon to call the attention of the minister to one or two problems and, if

time does not run out, to suggest solutions to some of these problems. I should like the minister to consider what I have to say very seriously.
Having said this, may I go on immediately to the main point I wish to discuss this afternoon, that is, the slow movement of grain in the western provinces. Only a few moments ago I heard a minister say there was no slow movement of grain. But I want to say this: No one in this chamber knows better than I do about this slow movement of grain, because in my own home town there is now a two bushel quota which represents the slowest movement of grain, six months after harvest, in history. In days of diesel locomotives, jet planes, messages from the moon and so on, this is simply not good enough. The minister who spoke earlier does not seem to realize that such a situation exists. Actually in six months one could have moved that quantity of grain by pack train or covered wagon train.
What is the situation today? The Minister of Transport knows about it. He has been trying to do something about it, and I give him credit for it. The real situation today in western Canada is simply this: There are half empty grain terminals; there are empty boats waiting; there are ships leaving for United States ports. This is a fact. On the other hand, the railroads say they have thousands of loaded box cars with grain and that these are waiting to be emptied at the terminal and loaded on the boats.
Today we must face the fact that this has been the slowest movement of grain in history. I ask the minister, in all sincerity: what is the answer? Someone is to blame. We-and I use this word broadly, speaking from the viewpoint of western farmers-have blamed the railways, the elevator companies, even the unions. We follow the proceedings in this house. One minister says one thing and another minister says another. I am trying to get the answer. I am not trying to be unduly critical. There is precedent. Later I intend to put forward a solution, or back up a possible solution which has been suggested by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle.
This is a situation we have to face. There are three ministries involved. The railways and the elevator companies are involved, together with the harbour authorities and about fifteen other agencies. What does it take to solve a problem of this kind? Again I refer to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle. There is precedent, as I mentioned earlier.

We had an indication of this sort of thing during the time when my hon. friend was the responsible minister in another government. He acted very quickly.
I would make this suggestion to the minister: Perhaps it is the railways; perhaps the holdup is in his department. Perhaps it is the grain companies under another ministry; perhaps it is an agricultural problem for which the Minister of Agriculture has responsibility. I would make a real and sincere plea to the minister this afternoon and ask him whether he does not think that it takes someone with the integrity and the prestige of a minister of the government of Canada to determine where the fault lies and what should be done to correct it.
Alternatively we might think of something else. I do not like this very well, but we have reached a deplorable state of affairs, with everyone running around and saying: It is not my fault, the facts are not as they are reported to be. But they are. It is such a deplorable situation that if it were not so serious it would be funny. How could we get into such a position in this day and age?
This is a grave matter for the western provinces. It is most serious in my own area of southern Alberta. Sales have been lost to the tune of at least $100 million. Hon. members can imagine what this means by the time this wealth has spread through the community. Actually the loss to the economy is about twice the sum I have mentioned-and $200 million isn't hay. I have read that someone asked in this house: "What's a million?" Believe me, a million dollars is a lot of money, and $200 million is just 200 times as much.
We come back to the suggested solution that I want to support. I do not think it will be necessary, because I believe the minister now sitting opposite me may well be the one with the stature to put an end to this sort of thing immediately. I know personally about this situation because I was down in the state of Washington at Pasco, which is 400 miles by barge from Portland. It was my desire to speak on this matter under the estimates of the Department of External Affairs so that I could express my thanks and appreciation to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the quiet efficiency with which he has operated during the past 12 months to make certain that solutions were provided for the terrific problem of low water levels on Lake Ontario.
I make no apology for discussing this matter under the estimates of the Department of Transport because surely lake shipping and riverboat shipping, to say nothing of the salties that come in from the ocean and go out, can properly be considered during debate on the estimates of this department.
During the months of February, March, April and May of last year I and several other members rose to draw the government's attention to the alarming situation that existed whereby the Montreal Gazette was able to
February 9, 1966

state that the water level in Montreal harbour was at the lowest point in the records of Montreal harbour statistics. I pointed out that the water level in the harbour at Toronto in February of 1965 was within one quarter inch of the all-time low.

I do not know how many righteous men were within sound of his voice when he spoke, but quite a few people are aware of the fact that there are two control dams on the river at Iroquois and Cornwall, Ontario and they could not figure out why the water level of Lake Ontario was dropping, dropping, dropping when, for the first time in history, there were dams across the St. Lawrence River that could maintain the water at any predetermined level if the operation of the dams was so conducted that the level of Lake Ontario would be held steady. This was a new expression to us, "Come up on the first steady, walk along the ridge and come down on the third steady". Being inquisitive we asked the old gentleman what he meant. He informed us that in Newfoundland where the water flow is small on many streams it is their practice to build small log dams every three or four miles on these small streams. water to carry them. The pulp logs are put into the upper steady, as they call it; the dam is breached, the water goes into the lower steady and the pulp logs float downstream to the mills. He said the word "steady" was used because the water remains calm and level as long as the dams are not breached to let the pulp logs go through.
I was fascinated by this Newfoundland term "steady" which, by the way, you will not find in any books on Newfoundland dialect-although I spoke to the Newfoundland members of this house and they told me it was well known and frequently used. I like the word "steady" because I believe that the Great Lakes system should be a system of steadies in the same manner the Newfoundland people use them to retain the water on their streams. If we had dams at the mouth of every one of the Great Lakes we could hold them steady and we would not hear complaints about low water levels at any time. We could restrain the water and maintain the level at any depth we wanted.
On thinking about this expression "steady" I wondered why in February of last year the level of Lake Ontario was at the lowest point, but for one quarter of an inch, in our recorded history, and I made some investigation of the matter. Unfortunately I can tell you that what I discovered was not at all pleasing or satisfactory.
I do believe that the uproar created by people interested in maintaining a satisfactory water level in Lake Ontario reached the receptive ears on the head of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because I am able to stand before you today and tell you that the water level in the harbour at Toronto as at February 3 was 244.02 feet, according to international Great Lakes data, compared to 241.32 feet, international Great Lakes data as at February 3 a year ago. This is an increase of 2.7 feet in one year.
Without doubt someone is going to say that the prayers of the minister must have been very effective. No doubt those people living on the shores of the Great Lakes, and particularly those people on the shores of Lake Ontario, were praying and working to improve the water level of a year ago; but, to find how effective the prayers of the public might have been, this morning I obtained by long distance telephone from the headquarters of the meteorological services of the dominion government the rainfall figure for the Great Lakes basin for the last three years. I took the rainfall figures for the Great

February 9, 1966
Supply-Transport
Lakes basin because Lake Ontario is the last receptacle for all the water going through the Great Lakes.
I obtained these figures not two hours ago, as the calculations made by the United States army corps of engineers and the meteorological services of the dominion government, and they indicate the following rainfalls: The rainfall in the Great Lakes basin in 1963 was 26.01 inches. In 1964 the rainfall was 31.27 inches, and in 1965 it was 35.57 inches. You will immediately ejaculate: Heavens above, the heavy rainfall in 1965 solved our problems, because 9.56 inches more fell in 1965 than in 1963. I want to draw your attention to this fact: The average rainfall on the Great Lakes basin from 1900 to 1964, a period of 64 years, was 31.30 inches, but the average rainfall for the three years 1963, 1964 and 1965, including the year when the minister was praying so hard, only averaged 30.95 inches, which is even less than the average rainfall for the 64 year period from 1900 to 1964.
I found that without any qualification the low water level of Lake Ontario is due to a combination of two factors. The first is that the people interested in maintaining a 35 foot level of water in the Montreal harbour were continually screaming that they must have that 35 foot level in that harbour and that the power interests at Cornwall must not be allowed to interfere with the downflow of water from Lake Ontario to Montreal. On checking into the operation of the Cornwall dams-and I went through these power houses and talked about the operations, from one side to the other-I found that the Ontario Hydro and the New York State Power Authority, which acts for private interests, were quite willing to run all the water they could get through their generator systems with the plea that they were doing so to help maintain this 35 foot water depth in Montreal harbour.
Since I was born in Ontario, raised in Ontario and represent a riding on the shores of Lake Ontario I cannot say that my interest in maintaining the 35 foot level in the Montreal harbour is the prime interest or object of my life; but this is a national problem and I belong to this national house of representatives, so I should give this some thought. But I do believe that I am entitled to give first thought to the people who live in the Lake Ontario basin.
I went down to Montreal where my father was born and where my grandparents are buried-this is a city I know well-and made

inquiries as to why they did not restrain, or retain the water that flows past Montreal in order to maintain the 35 feet of harbour depth. The answers I received are really terrific. It seems there was a 35 foot depth of water in the harbour when Jacques Cartier went by, and therefore there should be 35 feet of water there for the rest of time: Champlain said there should be a 35 foot depth of water in Montreal harbour, therefore it is necessary. One can talk about nebulous answers, but there are some.
I made a study of this question of harbour depths and I am indebted to the gentleman who first drew my attention to the great harbours of London, England, and Rotterdam. In Great Britain the main trade of that city was built up first and foremost by fleets of small sailing boats that were built to come up the estuary of the Thames to London where docks were built for them. About 1850 steam was developed as a source of power and they began to put steam engines into boats. Of course these were little steam engines for little boats; but within a very short space of time, as the steam engines in the boats, were more highly developed, the boats became larger and their draughts increased. It was found that as the boats increased in size they carried bigger loads from further away by steam, compared to wind blown sailing vessels, and that these boats could not go up the estuary of the Thames to London, particularly during low tide. As a result, the bigger the boats became, the more often they had to stand off London harbour to be lightered into the harbour.
After some years of this the businessmen of Great Britain decided it was ridiculous to have so much money invested in the harbour and docks at London and ocean going vessels not be able to use them. So the idea was developed that they should dig tremendous pools in the Thames right at London, in those marshes with which many of you are familiar, and put lock gates on these pools. They put gates on several deep pools and could then maintain the water levels as deep as they wanted, starting at 20 feet, and going up to 28 feet, 35 feet, 40 feet and so on. The big boats came in at high tide, moved into these lock harbours, the gates were shut behind them and when the tide went out from London the big boats were still floating in 40 or 45 feet of water, and were able to use the docks that had been built over many, many years at great expense and effort. Today you have in London the largest area of impounded water in the world.

[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The Dutch are a brilliant people and particularly good businessmen. In order to make Rotterdam a great harbour-and it is inland from the North Sea-they copied the British system and excavated down to the point where they get 45 feet of water in Rotterdam harbour. But it is behind lock gates, and when high tide comes into Rotterdam harbour the big boats float in; they go into the harbour and the lock gates shut behind them when the tide goes out. The water level is low but boats are floating level and can load and unload. Then when the big boats go out the lock gates are opened and the water level is maintained.
I made the suggestion in Montreal, "Why in the world do you let the water run loose and free down the St. Lawrence?" The answer was, "Well, it always will and it always should". Last June a meeting was held in Montreal by the Montreal harbour authority to discuss the water levels of Montreal harbour. In Montreal harbour this is the prime question.
The Montreal Gazette said this question was of national importance and something should be done about it immediately. I have in my hand an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of Friday, May 28. This article refers to the fact that the water level in the harbour of Montreal had reached its lowest recorded point in history.
At the water levels conference held in June a year ago because of such facts, I was given the opportunity of speaking. I was glad to have that opportunity because the proper place to make a suggestion was in the City of Montreal. I went to speak in Montreal before 300 or 400 businessmen of the first water, if I may be pardoned a pun. I said that the only way they could maintain 35 feet of water in Montreal harbour, or 40 feet or 50 feet if they wanted it, was to build a dam, preferably at Boucherville. I said Boucherville because it is away at the eastern end of Montreal Island and if they had a dam there it could restrain the water of the St. Lawrence River rushing heedlessly and needlessly by the City of Montreal, and they could have as great a depth of water as they wanted, the same as they have in London, Rotterdam or Antwerp.
The reaction to my remarks was most interesting. One gentleman introduced himself as the mayor of Montreal East, I believe. He came up to me after I sat down and was terrifically upset. He informed me that the
Supply-Transport
City of Montreal could not adopt my suggestion with regard to a dam at Boucherville because, he said, "If you build a dam at Boucherville the city of Montreal East-and it has 40,000 inhabitants-would be drowned in a sea of sewage". I said two things. I said, "What did you say, my friend?" He again informed me that if there was a dam across the St. Lawrence River at Boucherville the city of Montreal East would be drowned in a sea of sewage. I could not comprehend this because I thought Montreal treated sewage like every other civilized country and city in the world, and I began to make inquiries.
Referring back to the editorial that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of Friday, May 28, you find these words:
It has been suggested that Montreal should conserve its water supply to a greater extent by delaying its flow below the port . . .
But suggestions that the flow of water should be delayed even by the erection of locks below Montreal are not realistic. The problems of pollution involved in delaying the outflow to that extent, and the very fact that Montreal would cease to be an ocean port, open to the sea, and would become an inland water port, behind locks, makes the proposal futile.
This is the reaction of the Montreal Gazette. Then we have the Montreal Star of Wednesday, June 16. You will notice that the Montreal Gazette just refers to the problem of pollution. It does not say whether that is because people are emptying their fountain pens in the river, are spitting in the river, or are going for a swim there in the months of July and August; it just says that the problems of pollution take first priority. The Montreal Star of Wednesday, June 16, contained an editorial headed "Narrow Outlook", and says:
The solution proposed by R. B. Cowan, Liberal M.P. for York-Humber, for Montreal harbour's low water-levels-"Dam it"-undoubtedly has some sense, and, in effect, weirs downstream near Sorel, are meant to do just that.
But the idea is completely unacceptable because, to judge from his statements at the one-day symposium on water-levels sponsored by the Montreal Port Council, it seems to stem from a notion that much water is pouring uselessly past Montreal to the sea and that this water really belongs to the people around the headwaters of the St. Lawrence River.
People around the lakes too often think that the only problem to be solved relates to water levels, both in the Lakes and in Montreal Harbour,-
Please note this:
-and that flow-past has nothing to do with Montreal. The fact of the matter is that Montreal has a right not only to enough water to maintain shipping levels in the port, but also to maintain normal flow-past.

February 9, 1966
Supply-Transport
You will notice there is reference to "normal flow-past". This editorial continues:
The fact that both harbour levels and flow-past must be maintained are indications of the complexity of the country's growing water problem. Simple solutions such as this are evidence of an all-too narrow outlook.
I thought I made a very useful suggestion, because at Boucherville the St. Lawrence River is rather narrow and could be dammed quite easily. However the Montreal Star refers to flow-past. This is a new feature in international diplomacy, evidently. Looking into the question a little, further because of my curiosity being piqued by the mayor of Montreal East, I came up with a discovery that I did not believe possible: There is not a sewage disposal plant of any kind in the entire area of Montreal, Montreal City, La-chine, Laprairie, St. Hubert or any other city in the area except a town of 5,000 population by the name of Saraguay, and they have such a small sewage treatment plant that the engineer of the City of Montreal told me last Saturday afternoon that it does not amount to much.
I spent last Saturday afternoon walking around Montreal harbour. You will be happy to know that in Montreal, this great metropolis that is putting on a great exposition in 1966 and 1967 to show the rest of the world how to live, they just dump their sewage, raw and untreated, into the St. Lawrence River. But they take some pride in the fact that the great bulk of it is dumped in the waters known as the back river on the north side of the island, so the passengers coming in on the big passenger boats from Europe will not notice anything floating in the harbour of Montreal.
Oh, oh.

However, it appears that the load is too great to go into the back river and there are two sewers emptying into the St. Lawrence River on the south shore of Montreal Island.
I was at the Papineau Avenue sewer on Saturday afternoon for about an hour. These sewers empty into the St. Lawrence River through pipes with a diameter of about eight feet, and they hit the St. Mary's current in the St. Lawrence River and are whipped downstream in a hurry. I will never forget the taxi cab operator driving me along the shore in the harbour as I was checking these two sewers, which I could not believe existed in a modern city the size of Montreal and which has been settled since 1642.

I was standing on the cement embankment looking down there just above the Papineau outlet, and the taxi driver looked down there two or three times where the water became gray as the Papineau sewer entered it. He turned and looked at me and said, "Mister, do you see the papers?" And I said, "Buddy, I am looking, too; I am looking, too".
I make no apology for discussing the sewage treatment of the City of Montreal although I come from the City of Toronto, because it is absolutely ridiculous to demand that a flow-past be maintained in Montreal by using the waters of Lake Ontario. This cannot be justified on any basis whatsoever in 1966.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
In the Globe and Mail magazine of February 20, 1965, about a year ago now, there appeared an article headed, "Spirits sink over port water shortage", written by Robert Rice. I made inquiries last year and I found that Mr. Rice had been in Montreal for six or eight weeks, so he was a recognized authority on Montreal. In the course of his article, he makes this flat statement:
Lake Ontario, which holds Montreal's water, got the least of all.
He had ascertained that the rainfall was not uniform over Lake Superior, Lake Huron, Lake Ontario and Lake Erie, so this statement comes out:
Lake Ontario, which holds Montreal's water, got the least of all.
This was the first time that notice had been served on those of us who are residents of the Lake Ontario area that the water we were looking at belonged to the City of Montreal, and did not belong to the people who had decided to establish their families and homes on its shores.
The writer goes on to point out:
Nor are harbour officials and shipping men happy when an Ontario Member of Parliament, Ralph Cowan, a Liberal representing York-Humber, accuses Montreal shipping firms and Quebec power interests of draining Lake Ontario to suit their needs.
I do not accuse them: I just make the flat statement. If they want to consider it an accusation, well and good. I say to you that the water level of Lake Ontario should never go below 244.78 feet, international Great Lakes depth, because that is the water level average for the 94 years from 1860 to 1954. We have a dam at Cornwall and we have a dam at Iroquois. Why should we have to take water levels lower than the 94 year average of 244.78 feet? This was the average level for
February 9, 1966

that period of time when mother nature ruled the water level of Lake Ontario.
We have a situation now where an organization called the St. Lawrence River Control, which operates under the International Joint Commission, which operates in turn under the Department of External Affairs, is endeavouring to maintain the water level of Lake Ontario between 242.8 feet and 246.8 feet, that is a four foot up and down motion at this time. I maintain that they have no right to allow the water level of Lake Ontario to go below the 94 year average of 244.78 feet. If they want to use Lake Ontario for storage purposes, they can take the basis of 244.78 feet and they can use the high water mark of something around 247 feet, which was established in years gone by. To allow the level of Lake Ontario to go below 244.78 feet while relying on the prayers of cabinet ministers and the laws of heaven to refill the basin is a shocking basis on which to operate.
Now, the power people are going to scream that they are entitled to develop power at Cornwall because the demand is there and must be met. The demand may be there, but it does not have to be met. We have a treaty entitled The International Boundary Waters Act, which was signed in 1909. I have a copy of it in my hands. This treaty which is between Great Britain on behalf of Canada and the United States government contains a table of priorities for the use of water. In this table the priorities are spelled out. No. 1 is use for domestic and sanitary purposes, that is for drinking water or pleasure or health or washing or bathing. No. 2 is use for navigation, including the servicing of canals for the purpose of navigation. No. 3 is use for power and irrigation purposes. Please note that power is at the bottom of the list, and at the top of the list is use for domestic and sanitary purposes.
The people of Toronto want the level of Lake Ontario maintained at least at the average for 94 years, 244.78 feet. I am advised by an hon. member near me that Hamilton needs water, too. It is a dirty steel town. I have been over there with the Argo football team many times, and I know that Hamilton needs water.
You need a football team.

Of course, the Tigers wash us from top to bottom when we go over there.
The water level of Lake Ontario should not go below 244.78 feet. The City of Montreal
Supply-Transport
should instal a modern sewage system instead of just dumping the sewage in the St. Lawrence River, as it does now. We are told by the Montreal Star that nothing must interfere with the flow past Montreal harbour. This is about the same thing as a kid refusing to put the stopper in the bath tub when his mother is giving him a bath. She says, "Put the stopper in the bath tub", and he says "No, turn on the tap because I need a greater flow past". Well, you simply swat the little kid and tell him to put the stopper in the bath tub. Not so for Montreal, that great metropolitan centre which in 1967 is going to show us how to live in this modern world.
Order, order.

Shame.

My reason for objecting is not that I do not want the hon. member to complete his speech, but during the discussion of estimates there are limitless opportunities to speak. He will have ample opportunity to amplify the very interesting remarks he was making. My purpose in rising in this debate, Mr. Chairman, is to discuss an issue which has come to the fore in recent weeks, and which I think is of extreme importance, so that it should be laid before the committee. There are many other important issues affecting the Department of Transport, such as the problems of the Canadian Pacific, box cars and other important matters; but my colleagues, who are more knowledgeable, will be dealing with those issues.
I want to discuss the circumstances surrounding the application for transfer of television channel 3 in Barrie to Toronto. I want to examine how this has evolved. The whole thing is surrounded by an air of

February 9, 1966
Supply-Transport
political intrigue, as I think, and has all the marks of a piece of Liberal patronage. In my opinion, it raises very disturbing questions that the minister should answer in the house. It raises the whole problem of the new politics the Liberal party was going to practice.
The minister, I am sure, would be dismayed if he were to consult his Ontario colleagues. I would not disclose their identities, but numerous members have spoken to us and are extremely disturbed about the whole aura of secrecy that surrounds this application and the questions it raises in everybody's mind about a political deal. I want to deal with the subject under four headings: first, the move itself and how it came about; second, the interesting gentlemen behind this move and their connections; third, the whole political connotation that surrounds this particular application; and finally, the connection of Ken Soble and his application to take over CTV. In my opinion this also has an aura of political influence surrounding it. I do not believe the two things can be separated.

Before the hon. gentleman launches into his argument, I wonder if he would permit a question? He used the word "move". I am totally unaware of any move of any kind and I wonder if he would define what he means by the term "move"?

My interpretation is that an application will be made or has been made to transfer or make portable the licence in Barrie so that it can be relocated in the immediate vicinity of Toronto. This is nothing but a back door method of opening up another Toronto station.
And of making $3 million or $4 million.

As the Leader of the Opposition says, they will probably treble their investment. This move will probably be made without bothering to hold a public hearing so that all the groups who want to take advantage of this licence would have an opportunity of making their own representations before the board.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

I am sure the hon. gentleman, who made a very eloquent plea for justice the other day, would not wish to suggest that any Canadian citizen, who wants to make an application that any Canadian citizen is entitled to make to the Department of Transport, should be denied the right to

make it. Surely he realizes that the making of an application does not at all equate with the granting of one.

Mr. Chairman, I can see that already the Minister of Transport is getting uncomfortable at his surroundings here. Let us take a look at how this matter came about.
Mr. Snelgrove, one of the owners of the television station in Barrie, discovered what he thought was a very neat loophole. He discovered that it was possible to make his licence portable by applying to transfer it to Toronto. An application was made to the appropriate authorities here to investigate what they call the technical problems involved. After that was done the period for filing of applications closed as of January 11. So that no one even knew that this was being done. No one even knew that there was a possibility of another television station opening up in Toronto.
Everyone in the industry had been, and they still were, relying on the words of the chairman of the Board of Broadcast Governors that there would be no new channels opened up in Toronto until after the Fowler report had had the opportunity of being considered and appropriate government policy devised. In the background, under the table, behind the door, or whatever you want to call it, this neat little scheme was proposed and is presently under consideration. No consideration was given to all the other people who want to apply.
There are widespread stories that this particular station, if it is transferred, will blot out two of the major United States networks broadcasting into Toronto and southern Ontario. There is a difference of opinion about this. When Mr. Snelgrove was asked about it he said that Canada could not care less about the Buffalo stations. Well, maybe Mr. Snelgrove does not care about them, but everyone here knows there are about one and a half million Canadians who do watch these stations and surely they have some rights in matters of this kind. Surely it is not just a matter of sneaking this in by the back door without due regard for the viewing rights of the public.
Who is Snelgrove?

I am asked who he is. He is Ralph Snelgrove, a former Liberal candidate and one of the three owners of the television station in the City of Barrie.
February 9, 1966



As I say, this was all going to be done nice and quietly. No one knew anything about it, and no one would know anything about it. When it was all over we would have been confronted with a fait accompli, with a new station worth millions of dollars.
I would ask the minister to explain, when the opportunity comes, how a T.V. licence is made portable. How can a television station licence to operate in the geographical area of Barrie be permitted to come into one of the great lucrative markets in North America, the area surrounding metropolitan Toronto?
This is the way in which it was done. Mr. Dennis Braithwaite, one of the reporters who smoked out this deal, had this to say about it in the Globe and Mail for February 8:
The essence of their plan-
That is the plan of the Snelgrove group.
-it is becoming obvious, is speed, that and confusion-the latter being the special contribution of Ralph Snelgrove.
At the end of his article he puts the real issue in this way:
But the real issue is this: can a third station be granted in Toronto through the back door as a simple political reward from a government to three of its good friends?
I am not saying that that charge is true, but it is being bandied about. All through the press of the country allegations are being made that this is nothing but a political deal to reward certain friends of the government.
The very least that should be done is that if a new station is to be opened up in the area of metropolitan Toronto-and I do not pretend to be technically qualified to judge whether this is so-completely open hearings should be held. The whole matter should be opened to the public. Anybody who wants to make an application for a licence, and lots are now appearing, should have full right to make all the representations necessary. The whole matter should be exposed to the light of day, instead of being kept behind closed doors,' creating an aura of suspicion which is not only disturbing us here but is being widely circulated in the press. It also has 90 per cent of the Liberal members from Ontario very worried. Therefore it is important that this whole matter be examined very carefully.
Who are these gentlemen behind this scheme? First of all there is Mr. Waters.
Who is he?

I will tell you who he
is in a moment, but he is one of the coowners of the Barrie station and began oper-
Supply-Transport
ation in the eastern part of Canada. He built the CHUM radio station in Toronto, a very powerful station which plays nothing but rock 'n roll. He has a 50 per cent interest in Famous Players, Muzak in Ontario, and a substantial interest in St. Lawrence Broadcasting Ltd., which operates CKLC in Kingston. He has a 50 per cent interest in CJCH in Halifax. He also has a station in Peterborough. In fact, he has a very wide empire of ownership. It is also significant that he has proved to be and is well known as a Liberal supporter. The second applicant, Mr. Snelgrove, is one of the owners of the Barrie station and also has widespread broadcasting interests in Owen Sound and Peterborough.
The third person involved is Mr. Stirling, who began his career in Newfoundland with the Sunday Herald. He founded CJON radio and has two stations in Newfoundland. He founded CKGM in Montreal and launched CKWW in Windsor with Royce Frith, and shortly after Mr. Frith got his application he sold out and Mr. Stirling is now owner. He also owns CKPM in Ottawa.
What is happening here, Mr. Chairman, is that a concerted effort is being made by these people to build an empire of television ownership in Canada. This would appear to contravene subsection 4(d) of section 118 of the regulations under the Radio Act, which reads as follows:
Except with the permission of the minister given upon the recommendation of the Board of Broadcast Governors, no person shall be licensed to operate more than one station and no licence shall be issued or held by a company owned or controlled by a company holding a licence-
Unless they are Liberals.

In that event it should be amended to read "unless they are Liberal supporters". I think we need an explanation of this.
The minister asked about the political implications of this question. A very interesting article appeared last night, I believe, in the Toronto Star written by Peter Newman, in which he talks about the politics of channel 3. He names the three gentlemen involved. All three are well known supporters of the Liberal party. Snelgrove even ran as a Liberal candidate in the 1953 and 1963 elections. Peter Newman discusses the type of proposal that these three gentlemen are making in order to justify their application. He says, first of all, that nine ministers in the cabinet are opposed to the application on the basis that it smells of the very same kind of

February 9, 1966
Supply-Transport
patronage for which they so violently attacked the Conservatives when television licences were originally granted. He says the nature of the application is that it will not even likely go before cabinet and that they will not have a chance to register their disapproval.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
What intrigues me, Mr. Chairman, is the reasoning that these gentlemen are alleged to be putting forward for this change. The political aroma is strong when you consider that CKVR-TV would be the only non-CBC outlet in Toronto, and we pay to support the CBC.
The argument is that the CKVR station is the only non-CBC outlet in Toronto now owned by an avowed Conservative, the Telegram's publisher, John Bassett, who may also require dominance in the CTV network if the current application to the BBG for a takeover by the networks affiliates is approved. To offset this Tory influence, the argument goes, the Liberals should protect their interests by establishing a Liberal outlet in the Toronto market. That is, not a television station to serve the public, but a Liberal outlet. Surely that is the strangest reason of all.
Then he goes on to make some representations that many of us have been making for competitive bidding, for the right to serve the community, and he says in closing:
What's at stake is apparently only a television license, but the reform elements inside the Liberal party view it as a much broader issue: A testing of the 'new politics' which their leader advocated in the brave beginnings of his stewardship.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman that, wheth-or these press reports are true or not, they raise very serious and fundamental questions. They are making allegations here that all you need to have is a friend in the cabinet, or to be influential within the Liberal party, and it does not matter about the validity of your case, because you can get your licence anyway.
If we go to the CTV takeover, that question is surrounded with the same type of sleazy aroma, worked up by the press after investigation. On February 8, last night, in the Telegram, one of our former colleagues, Douglas Fisher, who has now joined the press gallery, wrote a column called "The CTV Takeover: A Liberal Test Pattern". In it he discusses, from his great knowledge or his

years in the house, several things, and he
says:
It isn't an accident that the majority of owners and executives in private broadcasting have been close to the Liberal Party. There was never anything as crass as the rule that one had to be a Liberal supporter to get a licence for a station or to buy into a station. But there was a general attitude that a party relationship helped.
Then he goes on to discuss the whole method of Mr. Soble's application, and how he was brought into the picture. Then he says:
This appeal-
That is Mr. Soble's appeal.
-is given additional savor by Soble's proven record as a Grit. He headed the Liberal party's broadcasting committee in the last election and he has on his channel given Liberal M.P.'s, especially the hon. Judy LaMarsh, continuing promotion.
Again, this important takeover is being enshrouded in the whole cloak of political patronage and political intrigue. I think it is important that we raise this issue. I think it is important that we lay these things before the committee, and that we get some answers back from the minister. I would appeal to the members of the Liberal party who are so disturbed about this, that they rise up and themselves initiate a thorough discussion and thorough investigation of what is taking place here, because too little is known. Everything is done in secret. The public is not being informed. The rights of viewers are totally disregarded, and the attitude is: We do not care whether this ruins the channels coming in from the United States.
The minister is quoted as having said that if Canada did not move into channel 3, Buffalo would steal it. Yet, investigations do not prove that to be true. There is no technical way in which BufEalo can do this. That argument is not valid under the circumstances.
Also it was never made by the minister.

If the minister says he never made it, then I accept that, although it was attributed to him in the newspapers. It was never denied up till now. Of course, we expected the minister's denial.
All I am trying to say, Mr. Chairman, is that this is more than just the business of television licences, because we want to know all the facts surrounding this application. We want to know how it got started, and why nobody was informed; why it was kept secret, and so on. We want some sort of assurance

SUGGESTED COMPENSATION TO ACCUSED PERSONS IN UNSUCCESSFUL PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Criminal Code so that an accused person who is eventually found not guilty may be paid his costs and expenses and such compensation as a judge, in his discretion, may decide to be fit and proper in the circumstances; also, so as to provide that a person who has been unjustly kept in custody for the reason that such person was unable to raise bail and who has been afterwards acquitted, may be paid damages and compensation for time lost from gainful employment and such other damages as are fair and just.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am bringing this motion before the house because I believe it deals with a problem that should have been recognized by the government of Canada long before this.
Although I am not a lawyer I am very fully aware that amending the Criminal Code to make this possible is going to take a certain amount of time and effort. However I say that, whatever time and effort may be required to embrace the concept of my motion and make it part of our Criminal Code, these must be taken, and must become law in a democratic country such as ours.
It is absolutely unbelievable and deplorable that our laws permit innocent people-let me reiterate, innocent people-to be held, convicted and later proven innocent, and then
February 9, 1966

Administration of Justice released with no compensation of any kind provided for them. Innocent people have been kept in jail for a matter of weeks, yes, months and even years; later they have been proven completely innocent of the crimes of which they were accused. An accused person would then be told by the courts of Canada, "We are sorry for our mistake. You are now free to return to your old job, provided it is there for you, or to your former employer, provided he is willing to have you. You will have to work much harder, of course, to endeavour to make up lost finances, lost prestige, lost health, mental and otherwise, and all because of our mistake-not your mistake, our mistake."
Do the laws that allow this to happen sound as if they belonged to Canada? I am sure we all realize that regardless of precautions taken by the authorities, innocent individuals may unavoidably become the objects of criminal prosecutions. The very fact that this risk exists makes it imperative that the public treasury bear the loss suffered by the unfortunate victim, and which has been imposed on him by the machinery of the law.
Today, with our country attempting to safeguard its citizens against losses caused by disease, disability, unemployment, old age and other misfortunes, it goes without saying that the state should be objectively liable for damages consequent upon wrongful accusation of a crime. It certainly would be manifest inconsistency in the system of law if the state, which guarantees the individual against losses in so many circumstances, should be excused from repairing the damage done by its own servants in the prosecution of wrongly accused persons.
It is certainly most unfair that a wrongly accused person should himself bear his loss. The prosecution should be at the public risk and not at that of an innocent party. It certainly seems far more reasonable that the loss should be borne by society rather than by the innocent accused.
Apart from financial recompense, an award of compensation might do much toward moral rehabilitation of the accused, freeing him from any suspicion which might otherwise rest upon him, despite an acquittal or dropping of charges. Also it might help in the preventing of prosecution of innocent persons, as it is argued that provision for such compensation liability should lead to increased caution and, in the long run, a decrease in total damages.


Right here in Canada day after day one can pick up the newspapers and read such headlines, as, "Wrong John McKenzie serves 30 day Jail Term-Does not get Word of Thanks," "Served Most of Sentence: Then Conviction Quashed," "Could not Raise Bail. In Custody Four Months; Freed After Testimony." In the last case it was really rubbed in because the presiding judge, Magistrate Joseph Addison said:
The most unfortunate thing is if you had had $500 you could have walked out free.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it seems we have two laws in Canada, one for those who have, and one for those who have nothing. Surely this cannot be continued in a democratic country such as ours.
I should now like to deal briefly with the famous case of the kidnapping of John Labatt III, president of the Labatt Brewing Company.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I would like to read you part of an address given to the annual meeting of the County Court Judges Association on April 23, 1964 by Judge G. A. P. Brickenden, of Simcoe, Ontario, covering his thoughts on compensation for wrongly imprisoned persons. In part Judge Brickenden said:
About 30 years ago, John Labatt III, President of the Labatt Brewing Company, was kidnapped. John Labatt was regarded as a very honest, straightforward man. When the trial came, Mr. Labatt said, in giving evidence, that the accused who had been before the Court, 'Kidnapped me'. He pointed to him, and any normal jury, knowing the fine reputation of John Labatt, would convict on that type of evidence.
During the trial, the accused was given 15 years, and he wasn't the kidnapper. At the end of two years the man who actually did kidnap John Labatt gave himself up and was tried for that offence. He was found guilty and given twelve years. The original accused was allowed out of the penitentiary and went on his way.
He went on his way to gain back what he had lost from society without any recompense from the government.
Judge Brickenden then said:
In other words, an innocent man, through an honest mistake of identification, served two years in the penitentiary without compensation from the government. I cannot, in a democratic country, see how this can be justified by any stretch of the imagination.
My contention is, that everyone who is wrongfully imprisoned, or who cannot get bail and is afterwards acquitted, should not only have compensation given to him, but also receive costs. This, as you know, can only be done on summary convictions; on an appeal from the Magistrate, the Judge has similar power. But, I think, the compensation and the costs should be allowed by the Presiding Judge within his authority, and make it

Administration of Justice from the Justice Minister... down to the last magistrate sitting on a bench in Canada, and every .iustice of the peace. It should also be required reading for the special committee on corrections-
The former minister of justice set up this committee to study the treatment of lawbreakers through all the stages of their arrest to final release. The editorial then continues:
The committee is to be advised by 25 experts of whom, curiously, Prof. Friedland is not one.

However, should this be the case it is my hope that legislation which will fully protect innocent people will be introduced into this house as quickly as possible after the committee presents its report.
I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the Criminal Code is strictly a federal statute and a matter of federal concern. I sincerely hope, therefore, that the excuse will not be put forward that some matters fall within provincial jurisdiction and others within federal jurisdiction, because this is a strictly federal matter.
I feel very strongly on this question of compensation being paid to innocent people, and stress again that legislation to take care of this problem is absolutely necessary. I sincerely hope that all hon. members will agree with me in this respect. Should the Department of Justice for any reason not introduce legislation to deal with this problem, all I can say is that they will be hearing from me in the fututre-and it will not be in private members' hour.

Well now, you know better than that. First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) for bringing this resolution before us. I am going along with him on many points but I wish to point out a few things. I can understand his concern for this problem, particularly as he is from the constituency of Norfolk which I understand is the great tobacco county of Ontario and that at one time an honourable lady minister was paying $600,000 of the taxpayers money to get people not to use his product.
But seriously, Mr. Speaker, I think the important part of this motion should be considered. If the judge, for example, was able to determine the innocence of a person, and
February 9, 1986	COMMONS
this proposal did not refer to all acquittals, then the motion of the hon. member would have greater merit. I believe that this question should be examined very carefully, because we do not want to bonus members of the Mafia or people who are acquitted on purely technical points of law.
If I may digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, I would tell this little story to the house so that hon. members may better understand my point. As I understand it, there was a certain lawyer in Calgary years ago, long before my time, who when acting in the capacity of defence counsel was successful in having his clients acquitted in 20 or 25 murder cases. When he was appointed Crown prosecutor, or the agent of the Attorney General, he immediately obtained six or seven convictions in murder cases. So hon. members can see that at times people can be acquitted when they are not really innocent, because of our practice of British jurisprudence.
A guilty person may in fact be acquitted of a crime, because of the burden of proof required under our law and the question of reasonable doubt. Law is not an exact science; it is not something you can decide in a test tube and be absolutely certain about. I have always believed that an accused person is fairly well protected because under our system of justice he has certain rights and remedies. An accused person tried before a magistrate's court or the high court with a jury has the right of appeal to the Court of Appeal of a province, and in certain circumstances the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
There are cases where the question of guilt or innocence is not cut and dried. I am thinking of the burden of proof required under our law and the fact that a case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. In nearly all cases it is a question of the credibility of witnesses, sometimes it is a question of identity, and the judge or jury must decide who to believe and who not to believe. Ten witnesses may say one thing and one witness may say another. The judge or jury, depending upon who is determining the facts, may believe the one witness and disbelieve the ten. Therefore the situation is not quite as clearcut as it may appear.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I believe that when considering this motion we must consider the question of whether an accused is innocent of the crime with which he is charged, rather than being merely acquitted

Administration of Justice of the charge. There is the question of discretion and the burden of proof required to determine innocence, which would certainly be a different kind of burden of proof than that required in determining whether an accused is found guilty or is acquitted.
What am I driving at? Basically this is what the resolution says, that-
-the government should consider the advisability of amending the Criminal Code so that an accused person who is eventually found not guilty may be paid his costs and expenses and such compensation as a judge, in his discretion, may decide to be fit and proper in the circumstances;-
The motion refers to "a judge, in his discretion", and this is the important phrase. I am glad the hon. member for Norfolk included "in his discretion" in the resolution. If this refers to the kind of legal discretion that would be used by a court considering the case of someone who had been convicted and had been unjustly kept in custody for a considerable period of time, or had suffered some other adversity because he had been kept in custody, and it was determined that the man was innocent, then I would agree with the proposal of the hon. member. But we must consider the question of reasonable doubt and the burden of proof in a criminal case, and if every person who had appeared before the bar of justice and had been acquitted was compensated or paid damages because of being convicted and held in jail for a period of time, it would indeed be a very dangerous practice.
It will be very difficult to decide these questions, and I was pleased to hear the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice, the hon. member for-I should know his riding but I have forgotten-*

Otherwise I would oppose his resolution.
In this context I am thinking of such men as Hal Banks, who was acquitted of two or

Administration of Justice three charges. Should he have been compensated? I am also thinking of a lawyer in Saskatchewan who was charged and finally acquitted. I am referring to Dr. Shumiatcher. His case went on for years. It is true that he was allowed out on bail, but during that period of time he could not practise law or carry on his profession. He was acquitted and I assume he was acquitted on the ground that there was a reasonable doubt in law. I do not want to get into that field, Mr. Speaker, because I had not read the depositions. I am not saying he was not innocent, but I am saying that he was probably acquitted on the ground that there was reasonable doubt in law. That is the kind of doubt that you use in weighing the facts of a case, the kind of doubt that an ordinary businessman applies with reference to any business matter. It is a real, reasonable doubt and not some flimsy doubt. It is a real, reasonable doubt which should be weighed carefully.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I know, of course, many cases are determined on that point. There are other cases I might mention such as that of Dr. Shumiatcher. These are cases along the same lines. Circumstances may change. A person may get a new trial or a witness may pass out of the picture. On these grounds someone may be acquitted because the evidence would not be there.
Many cases are very difficult to prove. One of the most difficult cases to prove and also one of the most difficult cases to defend is that of rape. Many times in these cases juries give a wide interpretation of the idea of reasonable doubt. They take into consideration circumstances that are not really spelled out in law. I know that, as a member of the bar, if I am defending an indictable offence of theft, a judge or jury will weigh the evidence in that kind of case and give an entirely different interpretation of reasonable doubt from that which a jury will use with regard to murder.
This is where you must differentiate. As 1 say, I would go along with the hon. member's suggestion, but there must be a legal discretion under which the judge has weighed the facts and come to the conclusion there has been an absolute miscarriage of justice, that somebody has been wrongly held. Otherwise we are going to have gangsters, members of the Mafia, hiring top counsel and being acquitted because they are able to get admissions out of certain witnesses or have a case dismissed on some technical point of law,
[Mr. Woolliams.l
suing for compensation. This is dangerous. I am not saying that the hon. member is one of these "do gooders", but I have always felt that we must take a strong look at motions put forward by people of this type.
The hon. member goes on in his motion to say,
.-such compensation as a judge, in his discretion, may decide to be fit and proper in the circumstances; also, so as to provide that a person who has been unjustly kept in custody for the reason that such person was unable to raise bail and who has been afterwards acquitted,-
In so far as the question of bail is concerned, bail should be set only at an amount sufficient to assure the person will appear for his trial. I agree with the hon. member in that regard. Too often bail is used by magistrates in the cities of this country to keep a person in custody in the hope that further evidence will be obtained. This is an abuse of the law, but the practice is followed in our cities in Canada every day. While we are on this point, another abuse occurs when a crime occurs and the police suspect someone with a record for committing crimes of that type. In such cases the police often lay a charge of vagrancy. The man is unable to get bail and is held on this charge in the hope other evidence will turn up.
In the meantime this man loses his job. I support the hon. member in that regard. Under these circumstances, I am sympathetic and I believe the man should be awarded damages. However, again I believe the award should be based on the question of a very real miscarriage of justice such as the example the hon. member gave where someone was held in jail for 19 years and it was found he was not guilty of the charge. I suppose if someone were charged, tried and incarcerated for a number of years, then later someone else came forward and said that they were guilty, that person would have been the victim of a miscarriage of justice. This person certainly should receive compensation. However it must be a strict miscarriage of justice in the sense of the person really being innocent, rather than a person escaping from the charge by being given the benefit of a reasonable doubt. Then I would go along with the hon. member in that regard.
We have other cases. You take the high court judge of the province of Ontario who was charged, and on his preliminary hearing was acquitted. This question is before the house now in a different way. I did not read the disposition of the case, but he may have been acquitted because of a reasonable doubt,

and perhaps a wide interpretation was given to "reasonable doubt". Certainly people of this type, Mr. Banks and the judge, as well as the other people mentioned, should not be compensated because they were incarcerated or charged and not proven guilty. They should not be compensated because they lost some income as a result of going through the discomfort of a trial. I am sure that is not what the hon. member had in mind in drafting this motion.
I should like to see how such a law was drafted before I would give blanket approval to the hon. member's motion, which is one that should receive the support of members. I will be brief, as suggested by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), and resume my seat.

My colleagues and I are in favour of the resolution presented by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh). However, I should like to make a few comments on it. One of the things that concerns me is the appearance of the word "judge" in the resolution. I sincerely hope the word "judge" includes in its definition the word "magistrate". Of all the criminal cases that come before our courts, about 90 per cent are disposed of by the magistrates. If the word "judge" does not include a magistrate, then the full impact of this resolution is lost.
The resolution appears to be a quick remedy for people who are unlawfully arrested or unlawfully charged with an offence. At the moment when this happens, the law does give a certain amount of protection. A person can bring a civil action. In some circumstances he brings a civil action against the arresting officer, against Crown counsel, against the magistrate and others. This places them in an awkward position. This resolution affords a quick remedy and also gives the magistrate the discretion to determine whether or not damages should be given.
In so far as this word "costs" is concerned,
I notice that a man who is found not guilty may be paid his costs and expenses. I assume my hon. friend includes legal costs because that is where the heavy part of the costs occur. One does not acquire too many expenses with regard to witnesses, but it is the heavy costs of legal counsel that have to be included. I quite appreciate the thoughts of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Wool-liams) with regard to compensating people who have been charged, but who have been acquitted because of the inability of the

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak as briefly as possible so that my friend the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), who undoubtedly has some interesting remarks to make about the resolution under consideration, may be able to take the floor.
That resolution makes for interesting reading because it shows the mover's generous intentions.
It is really terrible to think that some people can be the victims of a great injustice and to find with disgust, once the law has been proven to be wrong, that they cannot even get damages.
However, the same thing worries me about the resolution as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams). It could mean compensating a criminal with a record who, at one time or another, could be acquitted by the court.
In such circumstances, since we are dealing with hardened criminals who could be acquitted through some sort of hazard, would it be advisable to allow the courts and those who are responsible for law enforcement to give such people damages?

subtopic: SUGGESTED COMPENSATION TO ACCUSED PERSONS IN UNSUCCESSFUL PROSECUTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I clear up one point. This resolution has directly to do with innocent people who are jailed and then proven innocent. I am not referring to borderline cases but to innocent people who have been jailed and then found to be innocent. It is they who should receive compensation.

subtopic: SUGGESTED COMPENSATION TO ACCUSED PERSONS IN UNSUCCESSFUL PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for what he has just said, but the way the resolution is worded might explain why I am a little worried. It reads as follows: That... the government should consider the advisability of amending the Criminal Code so that an accused person who is eventually found not
February 9, 1966

Administration of Justice guilty may be paid his costs and expenses and such compensation as a Judge, in his discretion, may decide to be fit and proper-
And so on.

In other words, no distinction is made concerning previously convicted persons. The resolution merely speaks of people who are found not guilty at a trial
Therefore, that somewhat justifies the concern one might have in that connection. There is always the possibility-and this could happen-that a police force or some of its members who are corrupt would be only too glad to oblige mobsters by arresting some of their members, drag them into court, have them acquitted, and then compensate them.
I admit it is not likely to happen, but it could. As the saying goes, you can find black sheep anywhere.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, if this resolution is brought before the house, it is perhaps because of a rightful concern about the appropriateness of certain charges and convictions. As a matter of fact, the criminal code is supposed to remove all those apprehensions, because it provides that any peace officer or any person with reasonable motives-a person might possibly have committed an offence -has the right to lodge a complaint.
The following fact must also be taken into account. The peace officer has to swear a complaint. I am glad then that this resolution is brought before the house, because it enables me to speak my mind. Even though I have been practising law for a relatively short time, it is easy to see that too many police officers, probably because they are quite familiar with the court, do not realize the importance of their action and of their testimony under oath.
I do not mean to say that many policemen take the oath far too lightly, but surely one often notices that too many policemen, being too familiar with court ritual and proceedings, do not look upon their oath with all the respect and the importance it requires. That may explain why innocent people are brought before the courts. The person who swears a complaint should give it much thought for it must be done under oath.
What happens, because of court routine, is that policemen or peace officers are ready to sign any charge lightly, without a second thought, to bring any individual before the courts; when they are called as witnesses, they often have no scruples about saying Arhat they think.

This could explain why many innocent persons are brought before the courts.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make. I congratulate very warmly the hon. member for the noble intention which inspired him in introducing this resolution.
I thought, while first considering the contents of this resolution, that it could perhaps be an interesting case to refer to that famous ombudsman we hear so much about, if the resolution did not carry.
On the other hand, I find that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) has introduced a bill providing for the establishment of the position of parliamentary commissioner. One of the duties entrusted to the parliamentary commissioner by the law would be precisely those which the hon. member mentioned earlier. In other words, innocent victims who are dragged before the courts or innocent people who are unjustly condemned could be referred to the ombudsman or parliamentary commissioner if the bill proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer were passed.
Anyway, I congratulate the hon. member and I wish him success in his representations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that members generally would not hesitate to concur in the sentiments expressed by the hon. member in introducing this particular motion. Or, to put it more accurately, in expressing sympathy with the sentiments of the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) in his legislative aim. I would point out to him, however, that what he intended to do in proposing this resolution he has not done. He has not, as was observed a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Bow River, confined himself to those people who, as I suggested to him in my question, have subsequently been pardoned for not having been properly convicted under law. In the terms of his resolution he has referred to every person who wins an acquittal, which includes those who win an acquittal by a technicality on the indictment, or those who avoid conviction sometimes due to the nonavailability of crown witnesses or by other means which fall somewhat short of proving moral innocence.
The real question raised by the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, and it is for this reason I think that it is important to note the exact terms of my question, is whether or not compensation should be awarded where malfunction of law has occurred and where some person has beyond any reasonable doubt been wrongly convicted.
The hon. member has observed that he will have a great deal of impatience if one should refer to the division of jurisdiction in these matters between the federal government
February 9, 1966

Administration of Justice which enacts the criminal law and the provincial governments which except, in a minority of cases actually enforce it.
What the hon. member is referring to is a malfunction of the administration of justice. It is this area, with respect to the investigation of a complaint, which may involve criminal responsibility, with respect to the laying of the charge, with respect to the drawing of the indictment and the prosecution of that charge at trial, and upon any appeal, and in particular with respect to the withholding of bail, which concerns the hon. member and which the provincial authorities in this country are responsible for. What the hon. member is seeking to do is to impose a responsibility on the federal government for a malfunction of the provincial government.
I would suggest, if you look into it, that that is a subject which ought to be investigated by the provinces, just as the question of legal aid has been investigated in Ontario. In that regard the provincial government has unquestioned responsibility. I would suggest that it is not reasonable that the federal government which actually has no control over these prosecutions should have to bear the financial costs of the malfunction of law. This, after all, is a question of administration of justice and that, under our constitution, falls clearly within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
The hon. member made several references to the United Kingdom. He was unable to indicate what the provisions were over there. Perhaps I can assist the house by observing,

in this regard, that it is not the provision of the United Kingdom law, as the hon. member wishes to provide here, that there shall be a payment of costs in all circumstances. Rather, in the United Kingdom they have only provided for compensation basically in that type of case in which there has been a free pardon.
In respect of the remarks made by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) there has been a reference to the effect that under the resolution, a discretion is conferred upon the judge. I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of the house that as the motion reads the discretion is only as to the amount of compensation and not as to the making of the award itself.
